params.linkText: Akamai’s Anthropic Deal Puts $5.5 Billion Behind Its Edge AI Pivot

children: Akamai Technologies

is turning away some potential AI infrastructure business because of limited power availability, even as it has signed $14 billion in large deals this year, Chief Financial Officer Ed McGowan said at an event hosted by RBC software analyst Rishi Jaluria.

McGowan said the company’s pipeline is the largest he has seen in its history, with demand coming from enterprises, foundation-model developers, startups and other AI companies. But he said power constraints make it difficult to take on additional large projects requiring capacity in 2027.

params.linkText: Forget The Chips? Cloud Stocks Are The New Hardware

children: “Power is the most important, scarcest element today,” McGowan said. He added that availability should improve in the second half of 2028 and into 2029.
Compute Expansion and Deal Economics

Akamai has diversified beyond its content delivery network roots into security and cloud computing. McGowan said the company’s own rising third-party cloud costs, along with customer requests to run their code on Akamai’s platform, helped prompt its entry into the broader compute market.
The company acquired cloud provider Linode in March 2022. Since then, McGowan said, Akamai has more than quadrupled the revenue it acquired in that transaction.

Asked about an approximately 13% internal rate of return calculation for a large infrastructure contract, McGowan said Akamai included data center fit-out and network connection costs, as well as spare capacity, in its analysis. Those costs could be shared as other customers are added to the same facilities, he said.

McGowan also said the calculation assumed revenue only for the contract’s duration, although the company may be able to continue using the equipment afterward. He described the return as a floor, noting that a customer committing to a deal of that size receives Akamai’s best pricing.
Funding and Revenue Timing

Jaluria said Akamai had closed a $2.5 billion offering the prior week and was funded for its committed deals without returning to debt markets through 2028. McGowan confirmed that assessment, saying the company’s financing needs after that would depend largely on how quickly it chooses to grow.

McGowan said Akamai has investment-grade ratings from Fitch and Moody’s, while S&P downgraded the company. He attributed the difference to the agencies’ assumptions about future leverage and growth. He also said Akamai expects to deleverage over the next two years as it pays down debt and expands EBITDA margins.

The CFO declined to set a firm date for a sustainable return to positive free cash flow, saying faster cloud infrastructure growth would require more capital spending before revenue arrives. Depending on the pace of growth, he said, the company could reach that point in 2028 or later.

On recent revenue delays, McGowan said three large customer projects that had been expected to start in the fourth quarter are now generating revenue. Data center construction, customer-specific fit-outs and equipment issues can affect the precise date revenue begins, he said, calling it “spreadsheet risk.”
AI and Security Opportunities

McGowan said Akamai sees substantial demand for CPUs alongside GPUs in AI applications and will supply the hardware customers need. He also pointed to potential uses for its distributed infrastructure in latency-sensitive applications, including robotics and other forms of physical AI.

Akamai is already supporting workloads from central cloud to the edge, including post-training work, he said, but does not plan to build gigawatt-scale facilities for large-scale model training. Its development work includes making applications easier for customers to run without specifying the underlying hardware.

In security, McGowan said AI-related bot activity is increasing demand for bot management tools, although traffic volume does not translate directly into revenue. Customers are also seeking broader web application firewall coverage, he said.

McGowan described security as a healthy, recurring-revenue business but stopped short of predicting an acceleration in its growth rate. He also said Akamai would continue to consider acquisitions, while weighing potential deals against returns from investing in its fast-growing cloud infrastructure business.
About Akamai Technologies

Akamai Technologies is a technology company that provides cloud computing, cybersecurity and content delivery services. Its distributed platform helps businesses deliver digital content and applications, protect online operations and run workloads closer to users and devices. The company's offerings include web and application performance services, protection against cyberattacks, application and API security, and cloud infrastructure through Akamai Connected Cloud. Its services support organizations seeking to improve the speed, availability and security of their websites, applications and online services.
